claim: Germany’s Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said that Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn didn’t do anything illegal while at his German residence.
justification: The claim is **refuted**. Rather than asserting that Thailand's King Maha Vajiralongkorn did not violate German law, [Germany's Foreign Minister Heiko Maas actually warned in October 2020](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2020/10/27/asia-pacific/germany-thailand-king/) that any illegal actions by the king while in Germany would have "immediate consequences." His remarks came in response to [a parliamentary question from Greens MP Frithjof Schmidt](https://www.bild.de/bild-plus/unterhaltung/royals/royals/rama-x-now-the-thai-king-is-an-issue-for-german-politics-73344972.bild.html), who accused the king of conducting politics from German soil and characterized such behavior as [potentially illegal and incompatible with his residency status](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/people/article/3106641/germany-about-lose-patience-thai-king-maha-vajiralongkorn). No German prosecutors or law enforcement agencies [formally cleared](https://voi.id/en/news/16282) the king of wrongdoing, no other German officials confirmed his conduct was legal, and [neither the Thai government nor the royal palace issued any statement](https://voi.id/en/news/16282) acknowledging such an assessment by the German foreign minister. The evidence consistently shows that Maas's position was one of caution and warning, not exoneration.
judge_reasoning:
**Summary:** The recorded evidence clearly indicates that Heiko Maas, as Germany's Foreign Minister, did not assert that Thailand's King Maha Vajiralongkorn did not commit illegal acts while in Germany. In October 2020, Maas issued a public warning that any illegal actions by the king would have immediate consequences, responding to parliamentary questions about the king conducting politics from German soil. No German officials or prosecutors confirmed the legality of the king's conduct, and the Thai government made no acknowledgment of such a claim.

**Missing Information:** No further investigation is required, as the retrieved evidence consistently and directly contradicts the core assertion of the Claim.

**Conclusion:** The claim that Heiko Maas stated the Thai King did not do anything illegal in Germany is directly contradicted by his own public warning against illegal actions. Therefore, the Claim is refuted. `refuted`

claim: Officer who wore Trump 2020 mask to polls to face disciplinary action
justification: The fact-check confirms that Miami Police Officer Daniel Ubeda wore a Trump 2020 mask while in uniform at an early voting site in Miami, Florida, on October 20, 2020, an act captured in [photographic evidence](https://www.clickorlando.com/news/florida/2020/10/20/florida-officer-to-be-disciplined-after-wearing-trump-mask-while-voting/). His department, the Miami Police Department, confirmed the violation of departmental policy and state statutes prohibiting political activity by officers in uniform, with disciplinary action initiated by Police Chief [Jorge Colina](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/10/20/miami-police-officer-trump-2020-mask-poll-discipline/6001128002/).
judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check record, the key insight is that multiple news sources from the document store provide consistent, detailed evidence that a Miami Police Officer, Daniel Ubeda, was photographed wearing a "Trump 2020" mask while in uniform at an early voting site in Miami, Florida, on October 20, 2020. These sources confirm that his actions violated departmental policy and polling place regulations, leading to an official acknowledgment of disciplinary action from Miami Police Chief Jorge Colina. While the specific form of discipline has not been publicly disclosed, the department has explicitly stated it is being addressed immediately.

The only substantive conflict requiring resolution concerns the officer's identity and location. The document store consistently identifies Officer Daniel Ubeda of the Miami Police Department, supported by photographic evidence and multiple reports. The reasoner's memory-based answer naming a different officer and location (Chris Williams in Loudoun County, Virginia) is contradicted by the document store and lacks corroborating evidence. I am choosing to believe the document store because its claims are mutually reinforcing, cite specific sources, and include concrete photographic evidence, which the memory-based recollection cannot overcome.

Therefore, the core of the claim—that an officer wore a Trump 2020 mask to the polls and is facing disciplinary action—is clearly and substantially supported by the documented evidence.

`supported`

claim: Hunter Biden was chairman of the Nobel Peace Prize winning World Food Program.
justification: The United Nations World Food Programme did win the 2020 [Nobel Peace Prize](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/world-food-program-wins-2020-nobel-peace-prize-n1242678), but its governance does not include a "chairman" position. While Hunter Biden was [Board Chairman of World Food Program USA](https://sanantonioreport.org/before-hunter-biden-there-was-billy-carter-neil-bush-and-others/world-food-program-usas-annual-mcgovern-dole-leadership-award-ceremony/), a distinct U.S.-based nonprofit that supports the UN agency, he held no official leadership role within the United Nations World Food Programme itself. The claim therefore incorrectly conflates his role with the Nobel-winning organization, leading to the verdict of REFUTED.
judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the key finding is that the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020, but it does not have a position called "chairman." Evidence shows Hunter Biden served as Board Chairman of "World Food Program USA," a separate U.S.-based nonprofit that supports the UN WFP, not of the UN entity itself. However, a conflict exists regarding Hunter Biden's affiliation: one source confirms his role at World Food Program USA, while another working from memory has no record of this. Given the documentary evidence (including a source noting his 2016 speech and a Getty Images caption), I choose to believe the documented information about his role at World Food Program USA. This confirms a conflation in the claim between the two distinct organizations.

The claim conflates two separate entities: Hunter Biden was chairman of "World Food Program USA," not the Nobel-winning "United Nations World Food Programme." The evidence clearly distinguishes these and shows the UN body has no "chairman" position. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

claim: Joe and Jill Biden's income has increased recently.
justification: Publicly released tax returns confirm that Joe and Jill Biden's income increased substantially after leaving the Vice Presidency in January 2017. Their adjusted gross income rose from approximately $396,000 in 2016 to about [$11 million in 2017 and $4.6 million in 2018](https://www.cnbc.com/2019/07/09/joe-biden-releases-tax-returns-during-2020-democratic-primary.html), with the spike primarily driven by sales of Joe Biden's book *Promise Me, Dad* and paid speaking engagements, as documented by the [San Diego Union-Tribune](https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/us-politics/la-na-pol-2020-joe-biden-income-20190709-story.html) and [ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/joe-jill-biden-reported-earning-15-million-income/story?id=64225419). Their income subsequently settled to about $985,233 in 2019, according to the [Denver Post](https://www.denverpost.com/2020/09/29/biden-releases-2019-taxes/), which still exceeded their pre–White House earnings. These figures are nominal and not inflation-adjusted, though the magnitude of the increase would not be materially affected by such adjustments. No information was found regarding increases from investments or capital gains, and there is no indication that public financial disclosures as sitting president reflect rises in non-government income.
judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the key findings show that Joe and Jill Biden's income experienced a dramatic increase starting in 2017, the year after Joe Biden left the Vice Presidency. Their adjusted gross income rose from approximately $396,000 in 2016 to about $11 million in 2017 and $4.6 million in 2018. This spike is directly and credibly documented as being primarily due to lucrative book deals (especially for Joe Biden's memoir *Promise Me, Dad*) and paid speaking engagements. While their income subsequently declined to around $985,233 in 2019, it remained significantly higher than their pre-2017 levels. The evidence is clear and consistent on this substantial increase in the specified timeframe.

The claim does not define the timeframe of "recently." The evidence definitively covers the period from 2016 through 2019. If "recently" is interpreted as the years immediately following their time in the White House (i.e., 2017-2018), the claim is strongly supported. If it refers to a more recent period (e.g., 2020 onward or the last year), the evidence does not provide information, as the most recent data in the record is from 2019. However, given that the documented, massive increase occurred in the period immediately after leaving office, which is a common and recent phase of their post-White House life, the claim as stated is supported by the available facts.

`supported`

claim: A “new virus” disease called Novel Bunya V!rus that is caused by ticks is diagnosed as severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is spreading in China.
justification: The claim is misleading because while Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) is caused by a tick-borne bunyavirus (officially designated SFTSV, not "Novel Bunya Virus"), it is not a new or uniquely spreading disease; it has been documented in China since at least 2009, with cases occurring annually in multiple provinces. The term "Novel Bunya Virus" is not an officially recognized designation by health authorities like the WHO or China CDC, and there are no confirmed reports from China's National Health Commission or China CDC of an active, unusual outbreak as of the claim's date.
judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the key insights are: the pathogen causing SFTS is officially designated as SFTS virus (SFTSV), which belongs to the Bunyavirus family, but the specific term "Novel Bunya Virus" is not an officially recognized name by health authorities. SFTS was first identified around 2009 and is a well-documented, endemic disease in China, not a new or recently emerging virus. While SFTSV is considered a novel bunyavirus in a scientific classification sense, the claim's phrasing implies it is a newly discovered, spreading pathogen, which is not supported. Furthermore, there are no confirmed official reports from Chinese health authorities detailing an active, new outbreak or increasing spread of SFTS.

The evidence is sufficient to assess the claim. The critical discrepancies to address are the claim's characterization of the virus as "new" and its assertion of an active "spread." The evidence directly contradicts these aspects.

The claim is `refuted`. The fact-check establishes that SFTS, caused by SFTSV (a bunyavirus), is a known, endemic disease in China and not a "new" virus. The term "Novel Bunya Virus" is not an official health designation. Moreover, there is no evidence from official sources supporting the claim of an active or increasing spread of SFTS in China, which the claim implies is a current development.

claim: There is more chance of an asteroid hitting Earth on 02/11/2020 than dying from COVID-19.
justification: According to NASA's [Near-Earth Object Observations Programme](https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/what-is-asteroid-2018vp1-6568690/), no asteroid larger than 140 metres has a significant chance of striking Earth within the next 100 years, making the probability of an impact on any specific day — including February 11, 2020 — negligibly small. By contrast, even the most favorable COVID-19 mortality estimates, for non-elderly individuals in high-income countries during the early pandemic, ranged from roughly 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 2,865, as documented in a [PubMed study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32846654/), and were considerably higher for older populations. The claim's asteroid risk was tied to a specific date ([linked to asteroid 2018 VP1](https://www.iflscience.com/everything-there-is-to-know-about-the-election-day-asteroid-57074)), while the COVID-19 risk was not expressed as a comparable daily probability, and the disease's mortality figures were highly dependent on demographics, location, and time period during the rapidly evolving pandemic. Furthermore, only about 37% of near-Earth objects larger than 140 meters had been catalogued as of the claim date ([Planetary Society](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/neosm)), yet even accounting for unknown objects, the asteroid impact probability remained far below the established COVID-19 death risk. Therefore, the claim is **refuted**: the chance of dying from COVID-19 was orders of magnitude greater than the chance of an asteroid hitting Earth on that date.
judge_reasoning:
### Summary of Key Insights

The fact-check reveals that the claim compares two highly disparate and context-dependent risks. The asteroid impact probability for any given day, including February 11, 2020, is negligibly low according to NASA's planetary defense data, with no significant threat from known near-Earth objects for the next century. Conversely, the risk of dying from COVID-19 as of late 2020 varied dramatically by age, location, and time period; for non-elderly individuals in high-income countries during the early pandemic, it ranged from roughly 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 2,865, which is many orders of magnitude higher than the asteroid risk for specific vulnerable groups. The two risks are not comparable over the same time frame or demographics, and the claim lacks the specific definitions and context needed for a direct comparison.

### Information Still Lacking

To finalize the fact-check with absolute certainty, we would need a precise, universally accepted daily probability for a catastrophic asteroid impact on February 11, 2020 (which the evidence suggests is effectively zero) and a single, agreed-upon "average individual" COVID-19 death risk figure for that same date (which the evidence shows does not exist due to vast demographic and geographic disparities).

### Conclusion

Based on the recorded evidence, the claim that there is a greater chance of an asteroid hitting Earth on February 11, 2020, than dying from COVID-19 is not supported. The documented data shows the asteroid risk was astronomically small, while the COVID-19 mortality risk, though varying, was a real and significant public health threat in 2020, especially for certain populations. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

claim: Amy Coney Barrett has a written track record, disagreeing adamantly with the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to uphold the Affordable Care Act.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Justice Amy Coney Barrett has a documented written record criticizing the Supreme Court's legal reasoning in upholding the Affordable Care Act. Her 2017 law review article explicitly argued that Chief Justice John Roberts, in *National Federation of Independent Business v. Evidence from a 2017 Notre Dame law review article (cited in NBC News and Medium articles) shows she explicitly criticized the Court's reasoning in *NFIB v. Sebelius* (2012) and *King v. Burwell* (2015), arguing that Chief Justice Roberts "pushed the Affordable Care Act beyond its plausible meaning" and that the Court engaged in illegitimate statutory distortion. The key evidence is clear and consistent across multiple sourced documents, confirming the existence of Barrett's written critiques. No further investigation is required to verify the core claim about her written track record.

`supported`

claim: Ventura County election officials are reducing voting locations in order to limit in-person voter turnout.
justification: The fact-check concludes that while Ventura County officials reduced traditional polling places from 389 to 47 for the November 2020 election, this was part of a shift to a multi-day voting center model mandated by the statewide [California Voter's Choice Act](https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) and implemented in response to the [COVID-19 pandemic and efforts to encourage mail-in voting](https://www.mpacorn.com/articles/mail-in-voter-fraud-the-faulty-premise-behind-the-claim/). Officials cited safety and flexibility as reasons, expanded alternative voting methods with 30 drop boxes and extended early voting, and there is no evidence of an explicit intent to limit in-person turnout, with no reported concerns from monitoring groups about reduced access.
judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check record, the key evidence shows that Ventura County election officials significantly reduced the number of traditional, single-day polling places from 389 (March 2020) to 47 for the November 2020 election. This change was explicitly part of a statewide shift mandated by the California Voter's Choice Act, which consolidates precincts into multi-day vote centers. Officials publicly attributed the change primarily to the COVID-19 pandemic and efforts to encourage vote-by-mail, and they expanded alternative methods by adding 30 ballot drop boxes and extending early voting hours. Crucially, there is no recorded documentation, internal communication, or public statement from officials stating the reduction was intended to limit in-person voter turnout.

The information is sufficient to reach a decision. The evidence clearly shows the reduction in traditional polling places occurred, but it was part of a mandated state model shift, accompanied by expanded voting alternatives, and justified by officials for public health and efficiency—not for the purpose of limiting turnout.

`refuted`

claim: US state of Georgia has “almost 100,000 more COVID-19 cases, almost twice as many deaths and almost 600 more nursing home deaths than North Carolina, US.
justification: Based on the fact-checking record, the claim is refuted because the available evidence shows significant discrepancies with the stated statistics. According to the sources, Georgia had [39,801 confirmed COVID-19 cases](https://www.savannahnow.com/story/news/coronavirus/2020/05/20/georgia-covid-19-cases-rise-by-946-since-tuesday-to-total-39801/1173036007/) and [1,697 deaths](https://www.savannahnow.com/story/news/coronavirus/2020/05/20/georgia-covid-19-cases-rise-by-946-since-tuesday-to-total-39801/1173036007/) as of May 20, 2020, while North Carolina had [at least 22,725 cases](https://www.npr.org/sections/coronavirus-live-updates/2020/05/23/861561659/north-carolina-reports-highest-one-day-spike-of-covid-19-cases) as of May 23, 2020, and only [10 deaths](https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2020/04/01/coronavirus-today-april-1/) as of April 1, 2020. The documented differences are far smaller than "almost 100,000 more cases" and "almost twice as many deaths," and the nursing home death comparison cannot be verified because [North Carolina's data was not separately reported](https://carolinapublicpress.org/30369/dhhs-reverses-stance-on-identifying-nursing-homes-with-outbreaks/).
judge_reasoning:
**Step 1: Summary of key insights from the fact-check.**
The evidence retrieved from documents provides specific COVID-19 statistics for Georgia and North Carolina, but from dates that do not align with each other or with the implied timeframe of the claim. As of May 20, 2020, Georgia had 39,801 cumulative cases and 1,697 deaths. As of May 23, 2020, North Carolina had at least 22,725 cases, and as of April 1, 2020, it had 10 deaths. Georgia's nursing home deaths were reported as "more than 2,000" in August 2020, but North Carolina's nursing home death data was not separately available. The reasoner, working from memory, could not provide any corroborating figures for the claim's implied date (around September 14, 2020). Critically, the available data from the documents shows the difference in case counts between the two states was approximately 17,000—far less than the "almost 100,000" claimed.

**Step 2: Information still lacking.**
We lack reliable, contemporaneous data for both states from the same specific date or period implied by the claim (likely mid-September 2020) to verify the stated differences of 100,000 cases, twice as many deaths, and 600 nursing home deaths.

**Step 3: Conclusion.**
The retrieved evidence directly contradicts the claim's central assertions using data from a similar time period. The documented difference in cases was about 17,000, not "almost 100,000," and the death and nursing home data are either non-comparable or do not support the claimed magnitudes. Therefore, the claim is not supported by the fact-check. `refuted`

`supported`

claim: Viral message claims that all Haldiram’s food products were banned in USA
justification: The claim that all Haldiram's food products are banned in the USA is refuted. While a viral message making this claim exists, U.S. regulatory actions were not a blanket ban but targeted specific product shipments due to issues like salmonella, pesticides, or mislabeling, as documented in [FDA import refusals](https://www.medindia.net/news/haldiram-products-safe-for-consumption-food-and-drug-administration-of-maharashtra-151841-1.htm). Haldiram's officially dismissed the charges, asserting their food is safe and complies with laws ([ScoopWhoop](https://www.scoopwhoop.com/news/after-maggi-haldiram/)). Furthermore, the products remain available for purchase in the U.S. via online marketplaces like Amazon ([Financial Express](https://www.financialexpress.com/business/industry-jeff-bezos-brings-haldiram-to-us-customers-now-buy-bhujia-in-america-thanks-to-amazon-1755825/)), and no current U.S. law names Haldiram's as a banned entity ([Newsmeter.in](https://newsmeter.in/fact-check-viral-message-that-all-haldirams-food-products-were-banned-in-usa-is-false/)).
judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the key findings are that while there have been specific FDA import refusals for certain Haldiram's products due to safety issues like salmonella, pesticides, and mold, there is no blanket ban on all Haldiram's food products in the USA. Haldiram's products remain available for sale on U.S. marketplaces like Amazon.com, and fact-check articles explicitly label the viral message as false. There is no evidence of a total federal prohibition or a law naming Haldiram's as a banned entity.

The evidence is clear and sufficient for a decision; no further investigation is needed.

The fact-check conclusively shows that Haldiram's food products are not wholly banned in the USA, though some individual products have faced regulatory issues. The viral message's claim of a complete ban is therefore not supported by the facts.

`refuted`

claim: US President Trump opened a complaint platform to report censorship on Facebook, Twitter and YouTube.
justification: The fact-check confirms the Trump administration launched the "White House Tech Bias Reporting Tool" on May 15, 2019, as an official initiative hosted on a US government website to report perceived censorship on platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube ([Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2019/05/white-house-unveils-new-tool-to-report-censorship-by-social-media-giants/), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2019/05/15/tech/white-house-social-media-bias-tool/index.html)). The platform remained active until January 2021 and was discontinued after President Trump left office ([Vox](https://www.vox.com/recode/2019/5/17/18629426/trump-social-media-bias-complaint-form-facebook)). No evidence indicates the collected data was used to inform policy.
judge_reasoning:
The fact-check confirms that the Trump administration launched the White House Tech Bias Reporting Tool on May 15, 2019, which was an official platform hosted on a government website. This tool explicitly allowed the public to report perceived political censorship on Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube, and it remained operational until January 2021. The evidence consistently supports the core elements of the claim: the existence of the platform, its purpose, the platforms it targeted, and its origin under the Trump administration.

The conflicts identified in the record—regarding whether the platform allowed reporting for other social media, its specific audience, and the exact announcement mechanism—are peripheral details that do not contradict the central claim. The documented evidence clearly establishes the platform's launch and its focus on Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube.

Based on the retrieved and recorded evidence, the claim is factually accurate.

`supported`

claim: Some US mayors are fining people for going to church during the COVID-19 pandemic.
justification: The fact-check verifies that during the COVID-19 pandemic, some U.S. officials did issue fines related to in-person church attendance, with documented cases in [Chicago, Illinois](https://chicago.suntimes.com/coronavirus/2020/5/20/21265832/willie-wilson-pay-fines-chicago-churches-held-services-stay-at-home-pritzker-coronavirus) and [Greenville, Mississippi](https://www.salon.com/2020/04/15/william-barr-intervenes-after-mississippi-mayor-restricts-easter-church-service-due-to-coronavirus/). For instance, [Chicago's Mayor Lori Lightfoot authorized $500 fines for churches](https://web.archive.org/web/20210624060531/https://www.chicagotribune.com/coronavirus/ct-coronavirus-chicago-churches-fines-lightfoot-willie-wilson-20200521-y4mcdqlydjehdkzjbeh7rmhc4e-story.html) violating stay-at-home orders in May 2020. These fines were for violating broader public health orders on mass gatherings, not specifically for religious services, and their enforcement sometimes [differed from secular activities](https://www.salon.com/2020/04/15/william-barr-intervenes-after-mississippi-mayor-restricts-easter-church-service-due-to-coronavirus/). Legal challenges occurred, such as a [lawsuit in Mississippi](https://www.thedailybeast.com/justice-department-defends-worshippers-in-mississippi-fined-for-attending-drive-in-church-service) where the Department of Justice intervened, and community responses included [defiance and fines being paid by supporters](https://web.archive.org/web/20210624060531/https://www.chicagotribune.com/coronavirus/ct-coronavirus-chicago-churches-fines-lightfoot-willie-wilson-20200521-y4mcdqlydjehdkzjbeh7rmhc4e-story.html).
judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the fact-check reveals strong documentation of specific instances where US mayors or city officials authorized fines related to church attendance during the COVID-19 pandemic. The key finding is that Mayor Lori Lightfoot of Chicago issued $500 fines to three churches in May 2020 for violating stay-at-home orders by holding in-person services. Additional documented cases include fines in Greenville, Mississippi, where churches were singled out compared to secular activities, and legal challenges in Mississippi with Department of Justice intervention. While the fines were technically for violating broader public health orders, the documented enforcement directly targeted church gatherings.

The evidence from the retrieved documents is detailed, consistent across multiple sources, and provides specific names, dates, and amounts. In contrast, the reasoner working from memory had no reliable recollection of these events and in some cases provided incorrect information (e.g., claiming no fines existed as of early 2020). Therefore, I resolve all conflicts in favor of the documented evidence, as it is corroborated by specific sources while the memory-based responses lack detail and accuracy.

The claim that "some US mayors are fining people for going to church" is directly supported by the evidence of Mayor Lori Lightfoot's actions in Chicago, along with related enforcement in other jurisdictions. The claim does not specify that fines were uniquely for religious services, only that people were fined for going to church, which aligns with the documented fines issued for in-person services violating public health orders.

`supported`

claim: 558 people were killed by the police in 2018, while 201 people died in police custody
justification: The claim is refuted because the cited figures are not supported by credible data. For "killed by police," [The Washington Post's database](https://archive.investigativereportingworkshop.org/investigation/police-shot-killed-nearly-1000-in-2018/) reported 998 people fatally shot by police in 2018 in the U.S., substantially higher than 558. For "died in police custody," [INQUEST](https://www.inquest.org.uk/deaths-in-police-custody) documented only 20 such deaths in England and Wales for 2018, far below 201. No reliable sources corroborate the original statistics for the same jurisdiction and year.
judge_reasoning:
**Summary of Key Insights:**  
The fact-check reveals significant discrepancies between the claimed statistics and credible evidence. For people killed by police in 2018, a major independent database (The Washington Post) recorded 998 police-caused fatalities in the U.S., which is substantially higher than the claimed 558. For deaths in police custody, authoritative data from England and Wales (INQUEST) shows only 20 such deaths in 2018, far lower than the claimed 201.
